subject: biology
title: Antibiotic Resistance & Peppered Moths
welcome_lead: Today you'll see natural selection in fast forward — bacteria dodging antibiotics and moths turning sooty in just a few decades.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology Natural Selection in action — antibiotic resistance, peppered moths, pesticide resistance data interpretation.
final_note: You learned how a random mutation can sweep a population in 4 steps, and how to interpret resistance data for bacteria, moths and pests.

concepts.def: Drug that kills or stops bacteria growing
Ability to survive a drug or chemical that once killed
Bacterium resistant to many common antibiotics
Moth whose colour shifted as tree bark went sooty
Environmental factor that favours certain traits
Pests evolving to survive farm chemicals

walkthroughs.body_html:
A random mutation makes one bacterium resistant.

You take antibiotics → non-resistant bacteria die.

The resistant survivor reproduces. Soon the whole population is resistant. Same 4 steps, just faster.

Before factories: tree bark was pale. Pale moths hid; dark moths got eaten.

After factories: soot blackened bark. Now dark moths hid; pale moths got eaten.

In ~50 years, the population flipped. Selection pressure changed; alleles followed.

Tables often show % of pests surviving a pesticide over time.

If survival climbs, resistance is spreading. If it falls after switching chemicals — the new one works.

Tip: always look at the trend, not single data points.

mcqs.q: Where does the resistance allele in bacteria originally come from?
options: Bacteria 'try' to resist the drug
The antibiotic creates it
A random mutation
Patients pass it on intentionally

mcqs.q: Why did dark peppered moths become MORE common during the Industrial Revolution?
options: Soot killed pale moths directly
Dark moths were camouflaged on sooty bark so survived to reproduce
Birds preferred to eat dark moths
Pale moths migrated away

mcqs.q: How does a population of organisms become better adapted to its environment over time?
options: Organisms decide what features they need and grow them by force of will.
Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.
Individuals with advantageous heritable variations survive and reproduce more; their alleles increase in frequency over generations.
Individual organisms change during their lifetime in response to their environment and pass the changes on to offspring.

mcqs.q: Where do plants get most of their biomass from?
options: Organisms decide what features they need and grow them by force of will.
Plants gain most of their mass directly from sunlight, which has weight.
Plants get most of their mass from the soil through their roots.
From carbon dioxide in the air — the carbon in plant tissue comes mostly from CO2 fixed during photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: What makes antibodies effective against pathogens?
options: Antibodies are general-purpose proteins that work against any pathogen.
Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.
Organisms decide what features they need and grow them by force of will.
They have a specific shape complementary to antigens on a particular pathogen, marking it for destruction or neutralising it.
